title: Tenali Raman Tale 77

full_text:
A proud pundit named Vidyasagara arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he had defeated every philosopher from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. He planted a red flag in the palace courtyard and issued a challenge:
'Let any scholar of this court debate me on the ultimate metaphysical principle of the cosmos! If none dare face me before sunset, your Emperor must surrender the royal intellectual seal!'

The court scholars sat trembling, knowing Vidyasagara's fierce dialectical reputation.
King Krishnadevaraya looked anxiously at Tenali Raman.

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, I shall debate him right now.'
Tenali stepped onto the debate platform, carrying a small bundle wrapped in fine gold-embroidered silk, resting upon a silver tray.
Tenali placed the bundle upon his desk, closed his eyes, and bowed with theatrical reverence.

Vidyasagara eyed the bundle with deep suspicion:
'What profound scripture hast thou brought to the debate, Tenali?'
Tenali announced with booming authority:
'This, learned pundit, is the supreme southern treatise: *Trinabhimani Samhitasya Tritiya Pariccheda*—The Sacred Doctrine of the Living Blade!
Before we argue, translate for His Majesty the cosmic essence of this work!'

Vidyasagara searched his memory in frantic panic. *Trinabhimani?*
He knew every Upanishad, every sutra, but had never heard of this text!
Fearing that admitting ignorance would shatter his undefeated reputation before the Emperor, Vidyasagara’s knees began to shake.
He stammered, wiped cold sweat from his forehead, and whispered:
'I... I have neglected this specific southern commentary. I yield the debate to Tenali Raman!'
Vidyasagara packed his red flag and fled the court in utter humiliation!

When the challenger had gone, King Krishnadevaraya asked in wonder:
'Tenali! What divine philosophical scripture was inside that silk wrapper?'

Tenali laughed heartily, untied the silk, and dumped the contents onto the table:
Inside was a handful of common green buffalo grass (*Trina*), plucked from the garden lawn!

'Maharaj,' chuckled Tenali, '*Trina* is simply lawn grass!
The proud pundit was so puffed up with big words and complex jargon that a handful of grass wrapped in silk was enough to terrify him into surrender!'

The King and the entire court roared with laughter, celebrating that true wit needs no inflated titles to triumph.
moral: Arrogant intellectuals who brandish long Sanskrit titles are humbled by ordinary grass.
